claims.text: Friction stir processing with a pre-placed WC nanoparticle layer will produce an in situ metal-matrix-composite surface layer on a nickel-based superalloy.
The FSP-treated surface will be more resistant to hot cracking than a traditional fusion-welded repair or an untreated surface.
The FSP-treated surface will be more wear resistant than a traditional fusion-welded repair or an untreated surface.
The FSP-treated surface will be more corrosion resistant than a traditional fusion-welded repair or an untreated surface.
Pre-mixing WC nanoparticles with a binder will ensure uniform particle dispersion.
Pre-mixing WC nanoparticles with a binder will improve interfacial bonding.
A tool rotation speed near 200 rpm and traverse speed near 150 mm/min will keep the process temperature below the nickel-based superalloy melting point.
Severe plastic deformation during FSP induces dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement.
Well-bonded WC nanoparticles block dislocation motion.
WC nanoparticle reinforcement inhibits crack initiation.
The fine, equiaxed grain structure created by FSP increases hardness.
The fine, equiaxed grain structure created by FSP increases fatigue resistance.
Uniformly distributed WC nanoparticles reduce crack nucleation and propagation by obstructing dislocation pathways.
Avoiding melting and the high thermal gradients of fusion welding reduces hot-cracking risk.
The FSP-treated surface will exhibit at least a 25% increase in hardness relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The intervention will delay or prevent crack initiation under aggressive service conditions.
The improvements in hardness, wear, corrosion, and cracking behavior will extend component service life.
Traditional fusion-welded repairs use high thermal inputs that produce coarse microstructures.
Traditional fusion-welded repairs are predisposed to hot cracking.
Nonuniform particle dispersion or unmanaged tool wear in high-strength alloys may diminish the intervention's effectiveness.
